title: YUSEINOVA AND OTHERS v. BULGARIA
conclusion: Partly struck out of the list;Partly inadmissible
summary: In Yuseinova and Others v. Bulgaria, the applicants were six families—21 individuals in total—of Roma ethnicity, all Bulgarian nationals, living in the Hadzhi Dimitar neighbourhood of Plovdiv. Their case highlighted the acute vulnerability of Roma and Traveller communities facing forced eviction and demolition of their only homes, often without adequate procedural safeguards or alternative accommodation. Between 1991 and 2005, the applicants had built brick houses on municipal land without permits, but the authorities had tolerated their presence for years. In January 2015, the mayor ordered the demolition of their homes, citing unlawful construction, and gave them thirty days to comply. Some applicants challenged the orders in court, arguing that eviction would render their families homeless and that the authorities had failed to consider the proportionality of such a drastic measure or provide alternative housing. While the lower courts upheld the demolition orders, the Supreme Administrative Court eventually quashed the order against one applicant, referencing the need for a proportionality assessment under Article 8 of the European Convention on Human Rights. However, most applicants withdrew their complaints to the European Court, some reportedly under pressure from local authorities, and the Court ultimately struck out or found inadmissible the remaining applications. This case underscores the persistent challenges Roma and Traveller families face in securing housing rights and procedural fairness, reflecting a broader historical pattern of marginalisation in Bulgaria and across Europe.
